explanation: The veena was the chief instrument of Vijayanagara court music - treatises such as Sangita Suryodaya and the Carnatic tradition of Vidyaranya's Sangita Sara centre on it. Mridangam, tambura and cymbals were accompaniments.

q: In January 1565, the Battle of Talikota was fought between-
options: The Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccani Sultanates
The Mughal Empire and the Vijayanagara Empire
The Marathas and the Deccani Sultanates
The Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire
key_text: The Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccani Sultanates
explanation: Talikota (January 1565) was fought between Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) – not the Mughals, Marathas or the Bahmanis.

notes.text: - **Berar (Imad Shahi)** stayed out → enemy = **the Deccan Sultanates / combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda** (APPSC G1; UPPSC 2014) – **not the Bahmani kingdom** (already broken up), the Mughals or the Marathas.

q: Who fought the Battle of Rakshashi-Thangadi (Talikota, 1565 A.D.) which ended the glory of the Vijayanagar empire?
options: Ramaraya and the Imadshahis of Berar
The Adilshahis of Bijapur and Ramaraya
Veeranarasimha and the Nizamshahis of Ahmednagar
Ramaraya and Nizam Shah of Ahmednagar
key_text: The Adilshahis of Bijapur and Ramaraya
explanation: The NextGen Rocket Sheet records Rakshasi-Tangadi as fought 'between Adil Shahis of Bijapur and Ramaraya'. Berar's Imad Shahis stayed out, Veeranarasimha belongs to 1505, and the Nizam Shah of Ahmadnagar was only one of four allied sultans (he beheaded Rama Raya).

notes.text: - **"Who fought Rakshasi-Tangadi?" (APPSC G1):** **the Adil Shahis of Bijapur and Ramaraya** (Rocket Sheet wording) – Berar's Imad Shahis stayed out; Veeranarasimha is a Tuluva of 1505; "Ramaraya and Nizam Shah" names only the sultan who killed him.

q: Vijayanagara Empire was destroyed in Tallikota war of ________.
explanation: Vijayanagara was defeated at Tallikota in 1565 and Hampi was sacked.

notes.text: - **Date:** **23 January 1565** (some books 26 January) – year **1565** (APPSC FRO 2022, 2023; JL 2004; UPPCS 1993; MPPCS 1997) – not 1526 (Panipat I), 1545, 1555, 1560, 1564 or 1576.

q: In the year 1565 the battle of Tallikota was fought between them?
options: The kings of Vijayanagara and the Sultanate of Golconda
Vijayanagar kings and Kondaveeti Reddy kings
Deccan Sultans and Kondaveeti Reddy Kings
explanation: Tallikota (1565) was fought between Vijayanagara under Rama Raya and the combined Deccan Sultans (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) – not Golconda alone and not the Kondaveedu Reddis, who had gone long before.

notes.text: - **Berar (Imad Shahi)** stayed out → enemy = **the Deccan Sultanates / combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda** (APPSC G1; UPPSC 2014) – **not the Bahmani kingdom** (already broken up), the Mughals or the Marathas.

q: Which became the second capital of the Vijayanagara Empire after 1565 AD?
explanation: After Talikota (1565) Sadasiva and Tirumala moved to Penukonda, which became the second capital (later Chandragiri and Vellore).

notes.text: - **Capital after 1565 / of the Aravidus:** **Penukonda (Penugonda)** (APPSC G1 1991; G2 2000; AP History PYQ ×3) – not Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Kampili, Kondavidu, Addanki, Vizianagaram, Anantapur or Chandragiri.

q: What was the capital of Vijayanagara after the Battle of Tallikota?
explanation: After Tallikota Tirumala Raya moved to Penugonda and founded the Aravidu dynasty there. Chandragiri became the capital later, under Venkatapati II.

notes.text: - **Capital after 1565 / of the Aravidus:** **Penukonda (Penugonda)** (APPSC G1 1991; G2 2000; AP History PYQ ×3) – not Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Kampili, Kondavidu, Addanki, Vizianagaram, Anantapur or Chandragiri.

q: Which became the second capital of the Vijayanagara Empire after 1565 AD?
explanation: After Talikota and the sack of Hampi, Penukonda became the capital; Chandragiri and Vellore followed later.

notes.text: - **Capital after 1565 / of the Aravidus:** **Penukonda (Penugonda)** (APPSC G1 1991; G2 2000; AP History PYQ ×3) – not Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Kampili, Kondavidu, Addanki, Vizianagaram, Anantapur or Chandragiri.

q: Capital of Araveeti dynasty?
explanation: The Araviti (Aravidu) dynasty's capital was Penukonda, where Tirumala Raya founded it.

notes.text: - **Capital after 1565 / of the Aravidus:** **Penukonda (Penugonda)** (APPSC G1 1991; G2 2000; AP History PYQ ×3) – not Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Kampili, Kondavidu, Addanki, Vizianagaram, Anantapur or Chandragiri.

q: The Vijayanagara ruler who permitted Jesuits to build churches at Nellore and Chandragiri was
explanation: Venkatapati Raya II (1585-1614) let the Jesuits build churches at Nellore and Chandragiri; the Jesuit mission reached his court at Chandragiri in 1598.

notes.text: - **Jesuits:** **Venkatapati Raya II** allowed Jesuit churches at **Nellore and Chandragiri** (APPSC G1 2023; G1 PYQ) – not Krishnadevaraya, Achyuta Raya, Sadasiva, Devaraya II or Tirumala.

q: Which Vijayanagara rulers allowed the Jesuits to build churches in Nellore and Chandragiri?
explanation: Venkatapati Raya II allowed the Jesuits to build churches at Nellore and Chandragiri – not Devaraya II, Tirumala Raya I or Sadasiva Raya.

notes.text: - **Jesuits:** **Venkatapati Raya II** allowed Jesuit churches at **Nellore and Chandragiri** (APPSC G1 2023; G1 PYQ) – not Krishnadevaraya, Achyuta Raya, Sadasiva, Devaraya II or Tirumala.

q: Author of 'Sahitya Sudha'?
explanation: Govinda Dikshita, minister of the Tanjore Nayaks Achyutappa and Raghunatha, wrote Sahitya Sudha. Vedanta Desika and Vyasaraya are earlier Vaishnava teachers.

notes.text: - **Govinda Dikshita** – minister of the **Tanjore Nayaks** (Achyutappa, Raghunatha); wrote ***Sahitya Sudha*** – not Ayyappa Dikshita, Vedanta Desika or Vyasaraya.

q: To whom did Kshetrayya, born and raised in Muvva in Krishna district and author of erotic (sringara) poems, dedicate his poems?
explanation: Kshetrayya sang his padams for all three: Tirumala Nayaka of Madurai, Vijayaraghava Nayaka of Tanjore, and Abdullah Qutb Shah of Golconda, to whom he dedicated 1,500 padams (NextGen). So 'All the above'; the printed key named only Vijayaraghava.

notes.text: - **Kshetrayya** (original name Varadayya; "Pada Kavita Pitamaha"): born at **Movva (Muvva), Krishna district**; padams with the mudra **Muvva Gopala**; sang for **Tirumala Nayaka of Madurai**, **Vijayaraghava Nayaka of Tanjore** and **Abdullah Qutb Shah of Golconda** (1500 padams dedicated to him) → **"All the above"** (APPSC G1 2003).

q: Which of the following battles marked the real beginning of the Mughal empire in India and set it on the path of expansion?
explanation: Khanwa (1527) broke the back of Rajput power under Rana Sanga and let Babur consolidate and expand; Panipat I gave him only Delhi and Agra. Panipat II (1556) restored the empire under Akbar, and Kannauj (1540) was Humayun's defeat.

notes.text: - **Khanwa more decisive than Panipat (UPSC 2001 ×2):** A ✓, R ✓ and **R explains A** – Rana Sanga was a more formidable foe than Ibrahim Lodi; Khanwa "broke the back of Rajput power" and **set up Mughal rule on the path of expansion** – the "real beginning" of the empire (APPSC G1 2008 key: **Kanwah**) – Panipat gave only Delhi and Agra.

q: The Childhood name of Babur was:
explanation: Babur's name was Zahir-ud-din Muhammad; 'Babur' (tiger) was his popular name. Umar Shaikh Mirza was his father.

notes.text: - **Name:** **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad** (APPSC G1); "**Babur**" = **tiger** – he took the name Babur (CGPSC 2003); not Abdul Raheem, Umar Sheikh (his father) or Daulat Khan.

q: Who actually were the Mughals who ruled India?
explanation: The Mughals were Chagatai Turks (Timurids); Turkish was their mother tongue. 'Mongols' is the tempting option, but Babur looked down on the Mongols.

notes.text: - **Mughals were Turks** – **Chagatai Turks**, named after **Chagatai, second son of Chingiz Khan** (APPSC G1 2002; UDA 2010) – not Mongols, Afghans, Persians or Arabs; they called themselves **Timurids**.

q: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched?
explanation: Chausa (1539) was fought between Humayun and Sher Khan, so Jahangir - Chausa is wrong. Khanwa - Babur, Haldighati - Akbar and Bilgram - Humayun are correct.

notes.text: - **Kannauj and Bilgram are ONE battle (1540)** – lost by Humayun; **Chausa** was Humayun vs Sher Khan, so "**Jahangir – Chausa**" is the wrong pair (APPSC G2); NDA 2007: Chausa = Humayun and Sher Khan.

q: The longest Trunk Road constructed by Shershah which still exists is
explanation: Sher Shah's Sadak-e-Azam (Grand Trunk Road) ran from the Indus to Sonargaon in Bengal and still exists; the Agra roads were shorter Sur roads.

q: The Grand Trunk Road from Indus to Bengal was restored by one of the following rulers?
explanation: Sher Shah Suri restored and rebuilt the old Uttarapatha as the Sadak-e-Azam (Grand Trunk Road) from the Indus to Sonargaon.

notes.text: - **Hazrat-e-Ala first, Sultan afterwards = Sher Shah Suri** (not Bahlul/Sikandar Lodi or Islam Shah); his titles = **Hazrat-e-Ala and Sultan only** (BPSC 2000) – not Zill-e-Ilahi or Raiyat-e-Ala.
